notes: Complex construction adjudication enforcement; jurisdiction, natural justice, and severance analysis are explicit throughout.

enrichment.short_title: Enforcing motor speedway adjudication after jurisdictional shift on drainage

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: AWG Construction built a motor racing track and ancillary works at Rockingham for Rockingham Motor Speedway under an ICE contract.
Water seepage on the Oval track led to a complex adjudication in which Rockingham claimed about £1.8m for defective design and related losses.
Adjudicator Allan Wood awarded Rockingham substantial sums but AWG sought to set aside the Oval-related award for lack of jurisdiction and breach of natural justice.
Rockingham counterclaimed for summary enforcement of the award, while AWG argued the adjudicator decided a different negligence case based on additional drainage introduced late in the process.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court enforcement proceedings on an adjudicator's decision, with agreed issues on jurisdiction, natural justice, severance, and stay.
enrichment.outcome: Oval track award set aside for lack of jurisdiction and breach of natural justice; building and tunnel elements enforced for £54,328.73; stay application not pursued on that basis.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator's decision is unenforceable where the basis on which liability was found was essentially different from the dispute referred, and where a party was not given a proper opportunity to respond to a radically new case introduced shortly before the decision; where parties agreed to refer discrete disputes together, enforceable parts of a composite award may be severed and enforced.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator decided matters outside the dispute referred to him
Whether Rockingham's late shift to an additional-drainage negligence case breached natural justice
Whether severable parts of the adjudicator's award could be enforced
Whether execution of any enforceable part should be stayed

notes: Part 8 adjudication enforcement with clear findings on section 105(2)(c) and section 111 withholding notices.

enrichment.short_title: Enforcing adjudication awards after late LAD withholding notices at incinerator site

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: Conor Engineering subcontracted boiler and pipework works to CNIM at the Chineham waste incinerator and energy recovery plant in Hampshire.
An adjudicator ordered CNIM to pay Conor about £105,814 and £69,339 on two contracts but CNIM sought to withhold payment by set-off for liquidated damages.
CNIM argued the contracts fell outside the 1996 Act because the site’s primary activity was power generation under section 105(2)(c).
CNIM served withholding notices after the adjudicator’s 14-day payment dates, contending the final date for payment ran from receipt of the decisions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 8 Technology and Construction Court claim to enforce two adjudication decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Conor entitled to enforce both adjudication decisions; CNIM’s late withholding notices and section 105 exclusion argument rejected.
enrichment.ratio: On the facts, the Chineham site’s primary activity was waste incineration rather than power generation, so section 105(2)(c) did not exclude the contracts; where an adjudicator directed payment within 14 days of his decision, that date was the final date for payment and a valid section 111 withholding notice had to be served at least seven days earlier.
legal_issues: Whether the subcontract works were excluded from the 1996 Act as power-generation plant operations
What constituted the final date for payment of sums awarded by the adjudicator
Whether CNIM’s withholding notices were effective and served in time
Whether Conor waived or extended the payment period by later invoicing

ABB Power Construction Ltd v Norwest Holst Engineering 77 Con LR 20

notes: Short criminal appeal on affray directions and inconsistent verdicts; outcome and authorities are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Affray appeal on reasonable firmness direction and inconsistent verdicts
key_facts: Father and son appellants were convicted of affray after an incident beginning at the Black Horse pub in Otley and continuing at a nearby takeaway.
The prosecution case included a car screeching to a halt, attempts to force entry, shouting, and a door being kicked in.
Both appellants were acquitted of related common assault counts but convicted on affray.
They appealed on the adequacy of the affray summing-up and, by renewed application, alleged inconsistent verdicts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction by leave of the Single Judge, with a renewed application on inconsistent verdicts refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; affray direction held adequate and verdicts not logically inconsistent.
enrichment.ratio: A succinct direction identifying unlawful violence, its direction towards another, and the effect on a person of reasonable firmness can be sufficient for affray; acquittal on assault counts requiring actual violence does not make an affray conviction inconsistent where the affray case rested on threats and surrounding conduct.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge adequately directed the jury on a person of reasonable firmness
Whether convictions for affray were logically inconsistent with acquittals on assault counts

R v McCluskey (1989) 91 Cr App R 216
R v Bell (1997)
R v G [1998] Crim LR 483

notes: CPR transitional stay case with detailed procedural history and fresh discretion exercise on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Lifting PD 51.19 stay in long-delayed education negligence claim
key_facts: The claimant alleged Lincolnshire County Council negligently failed to provide appropriate speech therapy during his childhood, causing lasting speech impairment.
Proceedings began in 1993 when he was a child and were repeatedly stayed pending House of Lords education-liability cases and legal aid issues.
The action was automatically stayed under PD 51.19 on 25 April 2000 after no judicial activity in the preceding year.
In 2003 the claimant applied to lift the stay; the judge refused, but the Court of Appeal reconsidered under CPR 3.9.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to lift an automatic stay imposed by Practice Direction 51.19.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; automatic stay lifted with directions for mediation and case management; defendant ordered to pay £6,000 appeal costs.
enrichment.ratio: Relief from an automatic PD 51.19 stay falls under CPR 3.9; where a litigant in person could not reasonably have known of the transitional provision and major delay arose from awaiting binding House of Lords authority, blame for later solicitor delay should not be attributed to the claimant, and a fair trial may still be possible where the defendant has not shown prejudice from the additional delay.
legal_issues: Whether relief from the PD 51.19 automatic stay should be granted under CPR 3.9
Whether the claimant was personally responsible for procedural delay
Whether a fair trial remained possible after long delay
How an appeal court should exercise discretion afresh where the judge misattributed fault

Woodhouse v Consignia Plc [2002] EWCA Civ 275
Hansom v Makin [2003] EWCA Civ 1801

notes: Committal judicial review with clear rulings on computer printout evidence and incitement via automated systems.

enrichment.short_title: Committal upheld over Landslide child pornography portal subscriptions
key_facts: Anthony O'Shea sought judicial review of a Coventry magistrates' court decision committing him for trial on child pornography incitement charges.
The prosecution relied on Landslide Productions portal records showing registrations and credit card payments linked to his email and card details.
The claimant argued computer printouts were inadmissible hearsay and that subscribing through an automated website could not incite a human offender.
Expert evidence showed access required deliberate navigation, registration, and password entry rather than accidental connection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of committal proceedings with permission granted by the Single Judge.
enrichment.outcome: Application for judicial review refused; committal decision upheld on admissibility, sufficiency, and offence elements.
enrichment.ratio: Computer-generated transaction printouts recording automated portal activity are real evidence rather than hearsay where no human mind intervened in creating the record; at committal stage, matching credit card and email details can support a prima facie inference that the defendant subscribed, and payment through an automated system can amount to incitement of the human operators behind the business.
legal_issues: Whether Landslide database printouts were admissible real evidence or hearsay
Whether there was sufficient evidence connecting the claimant to the subscriptions
Whether subscribing via an automated computer system could constitute incitement to distribute indecent images

R v Goldman [2001]
DPP v Armstrong (1999)

notes: Dense employment and CPR strike-out judgment; acceptance of repudiation and abuse analysis are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Strike-out appeal on continuing contract and employment tribunal res judicata
key_facts: Miss Sivanandan, a racial equality officer employed by Enfield, was suspended and dismissed by EREC although Enfield was her actual employer.
She brought extensive employment tribunal proceedings for discrimination and breach of contract, later struck out for vexatious conduct.
In 2002 she issued High Court proceedings claiming continuing contract losses, mental health damage, and unpaid salary.
Master Leslie struck out parts of the claim; both sides appealed on termination, limitation, res judicata, and abuse of process grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Queen's Bench appeal and cross-appeal from master’s strike-out decisions under CPR 3.4.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeal and cross-appeal dismissed; claim for continuing earnings struck out after finding acceptance of repudiation, but narrower contractual loss claim allowed to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employee objectively acts inconsistently with continuation of employment, including bringing tribunal claims requiring termination and seeking wrongful dismissal remedies, repudiation is accepted and no continuing-contract breach claim can survive; withdrawing a contractual claim from tribunal proceedings to pursue it within jurisdiction in civil court is not an abuse of process under Sajid v Sussex Muslim Society.
legal_issues: Whether the employee accepted Enfield’s repudiation of her contract
Whether High Court proceedings were barred by res judicata or abuse after tribunal litigation
Whether claims for mental health damage and loss of earnings should be struck out
Whether a withdrawn tribunal contractual claim could be pursued separately in court

Boyo v London Borough of Lambeth [1995] IRLR 50

notes: Post-judgment order hearing only; points on injunction scope, stay, delivery up, and costs are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Patent injunction and indemnity costs order after Rockwater infringement win
key_facts: Following a successful patent infringement judgment for Coflexip against Rockwater, the parties disputed the form of the final order.
Rockwater sought to limit the injunction to claims 3 to 9 and argued dropped allegations on claims 1 and 2 should reduce costs.
Coflexip sought delivery up, a stay, a special liberty-to-apply proviso, and an interim costs payment of £1.5 million.
Rockwater had no infringing vessel within the jurisdiction and no current project threatening further infringement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal hearing on the form of order, costs, and permission to appeal after substantive patent judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction not limited to claims 3 to 9; no stay or delivery-up order; indemnity costs scale applied with £1.25 million interim payment; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where claim 3 is wider than claims 1 and 2, limiting an injunction to claim 3 is pointless; absent exceptional circumstances there should be no stay of injunction or costs assessment after a second unsuccessful validity challenge on similar prior art; dropped late infringement allegations on narrower claims do not justify costs reduction where related validity issues remained live.
legal_issues: Whether the injunction should exclude claims 1 and 2
Whether to stay the injunction, inquiry, or costs assessment
Whether delivery up or a special liberty-to-apply proviso was appropriate
Whether indemnity costs and an interim payment should be ordered

notes: Deceit damages appeal with detailed treatment of Smith New Court principles and benefit set-off.

enrichment.short_title: Deceit damages where hospital development gave no set-off benefit
key_facts: Mr Piper fraudulently induced Midco to invest in and lend money to Jesse Holness, an estate agency company he controlled.
Midco lost about £183,345 when Jesse Holness failed, plus personal loans to Piper.
Piper argued Midco should give credit for profits from a separate hospital redevelopment project funded through related companies Woodbarn and Keron.
At December 1996 valuation the hospital project showed a loss, although later values increased.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a county court deceit judgment on liability and quantum already decided below.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no benefit set-off allowed and full fraud damages upheld.
enrichment.ratio: In deceit, a claimant must give credit for benefits directly flowing from the induced transaction, and the venture induced may include wider property development not only the initial acquisition; however, where the benefit assessment date is when the continuing misrepresentation ended and the claimant was locked in, there was no proven benefit from the hospital project at that date.
legal_issues: Whether the induced transaction included property development or only the estate agency purchase
Whether Midco received benefits requiring set-off against deceit damages
At what date benefits should be assessed
On whom lay the burden of proving benefit
linked_authorities: Smith New Court Securities Ltd v Citibank NA [1997] AC 254
Mead v Clarke Chapman Ltd [1956] 1 WLR 76

confidence.notes: Liability was not in issue on appeal and the benefit/set-off analysis is thorough. Some valuation figures depend on expert evidence accepted at trial.

notes: Leading follow-the-settlements construction issue; Scor and Hiscox principles applied in detail.

enrichment.short_title: Follow-the-settlements reinsurance clause after St Lawrence cable claim
key_facts: Generali settled a Canadian insured’s claim for about $4m after power cables under the St Lawrence river failed due to abrasion.
Coverage disputes included unforeseen loss, proximate cause, design/workmanship, and single versus multiple losses.
Generali reinsured 80% on back-to-back terms including a clause to follow settlements 'without question'.
Defendant reinsurers refused payment, relying on both Scor provisos while Lloyd’s subscribers had paid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Commercial Court declaration on construction of a follow-the-settlements clause after summary judgment failed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reinsurers may rely on both Scor provisos and 'without question' did not exclude them.
enrichment.ratio: A standard follow-the-settlements clause binds reinsurers to an insurer’s honest, businesslike settlement but does not remove the requirement that the recognised claim fall within the reinsurance as a matter of law or arguable law; where insurance and reinsurance are back to back, reinsurers may still raise coverage issues under the reinsurance, and 'without question' emphasises non-challenge of admitted or compromised settlements rather than excluding the Scor provisos.
legal_issues: Whether reinsurers could raise coverage issues common to back-to-back insurance and reinsurance
The meaning of the first Scor proviso where contracts are co-extensive
Whether 'without question' excluded one or both Scor provisos
How settlements recognised by the insurer satisfy the reinsurance cover test

notes: Dublin Convention certification challenge applying Razgar and Djali; Article 8 analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Certifying Dublin return to Germany for Kosovan family

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: The Sopa family, ethnic Albanians from Kosovo, lived in Germany for about six years before entering the UK illegally in 1998 and claiming asylum.
Their asylum claim was refused on Dublin Convention third-country grounds in 1998, but removal was delayed by prolonged judicial review.
In 2002 they argued return to Germany would breach Articles 3 and 8, particularly for eldest daughter Tina’s psychiatric condition.
The Secretary of State certified the human rights claims as manifestly unfounded; fresh psychiatric and German healthcare evidence was adduced on adjournment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of certification decisions under the Dublin Convention return process, following permission granted after Razgar.
enrichment.outcome: Claim for judicial review refused; certification upheld for both claimant and Tina; defendant’s costs ordered subject to legal aid terms.
enrichment.ratio: Where essential facts are not in dispute, an adjudicator reviewing certification asks whether the Secretary of State’s Article 8(2) balancing decision was within the range of reasonable responses; removal to Germany after precarious unlawful presence and prior integration there is not disproportionate, and denial of psychiatric counselling in Germany is not a realistic Article 8 harm where medical treatment would be available if required to avoid Convention breach.
legal_issues: Whether Article 8 certification was lawful for the family’s integration in the UK
Whether Tina’s psychiatric condition engaged Article 8 or Article 3
Whether Germany would deny necessary medical treatment to failed asylum seekers
The correct approach to certification after Razgar and Djali
linked_authorities: Razgar v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 840
Djali v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 1371
Edore v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] EWCA Civ 716

confidence.notes: Human rights and certification principles are clearly applied to up-to-date evidence. Article 3 claim for the claimant was conceded and Tina’s Article 3 case was treated as unrealistic.
